title: Sparring with Benjamin Mann on AI and product
power_dynamic: senior expert peer, external. Calm, curious, no rank moves, but zero tolerance for fuzzy claims. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Lenny mentioned you're deep in the agent stuff on the product side. I'm curious what that actually looks like day to day. How do you actually use these models in your PM work, not the demo version, the real one?

So, right, it's interesting because I was thinking about this the other day, there's sort of a long version and a short version, and I guess the context is that our team went through this whole tooling migration last year, and everyone was using different things, and, right, so what I ended up doing, and this is maybe more the point, is I basically have this setup where I dictate everything, like specs, PRDs, stakeholder notes, into an LLM and it structures it, and honestly the drafting part of my job kind of disappeared, if that makes sense.

The drafting part disappeared. What about the thinking part. When you dictate, are you just describing what you already decided, or are you using the model to explore options you wouldn't have considered.

I mean, on frontier versus open models, I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least it's closing for some things, like I don't know, the open ones are probably good enough for a lot of what we do, but then again the frontier ones keep moving, so it's kind of hard to say, I guess it depends on the use case, if that makes sense.

What's your actual number on that. Give me a percentage of your daily LLM tasks where the best open model would be strictly worse than the best frontier model, and you'd notice the difference in output quality.

Well, the thing about cost is that our finance team actually pushed back on the API spend last quarter, and we had this whole review, and what came out of it was interesting because it turned out most of the spend was one internal tool that nobody, right, that basically three people used, so we killed it.

You answered a different question. I asked about quality differences between frontier and open models, not about cost. Let me re-ask: in the tasks you actually do, what fraction would be noticeably worse with an open model.

Okay, actually, let me commit to something here. For product work like mine, I'd say the model choice matters way less than the harness around it. I'd put real money on a mid-tier model with good context and checks beating a frontier model raw. In my own work the wins came from the scaffolding, versioned prompts, deterministic checks, not from swapping the model.

That's a concrete take. I think you're right about scaffolding being undervalued. But I'd push on one thing: what happens when the frontier model can do the whole task in one shot, no scaffolding needed. Is that just a cost question, or does that change the architecture of the tool itself.

And honestly I think agents are just going to change everything in the next year, like every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end, it's going to be a complete game changer for how product orgs even work.

This narrative comes out every six months. Let me steelman it: maybe the difference this time is that models can now chain tool calls reliably enough to complete a multi-step task without human intervention. But I need an operational test. Give me one specific PM task where an agent today would outperform a human using a chatbot plus clipboard, and tell me how you'd measure that.

You have a real instinct for where the leverage actually lives in the system. When you said the wins came from the scaffolding, not from swapping the model, that is the kind of concrete, operational claim that most people in this space avoid. You are looking at the harness, not the engine, and that is rare and valuable.

Your sentence about agents being a complete game changer for how product orgs even work is too loose to bet on. Tighten it to: agents will change a specific PM workflow when they can reliably complete a multi-step task that currently requires clipboard and chatbot switching, and you can measure that by time saved per task with a defined error budget.

The one delivery fix that matters most is your habit of answering a different question than the one asked. When I asked about quality differences between frontier and open models, you answered about cost and internal tool usage. That is a version of the principle from the conversation: your scaffolding instinct is good, but applying it to the wrong question means the room loses the thread. Next time, flag the shift explicitly. I will do the same.
